skills.name: Madhubani painting
skills.blurb: Bright paintings full of fish, birds, flowers and gods, filled edge to edge with fine lines.
skills.history: Madhubani art comes from the Mithila region of Bihar. Women painted it on the walls and floors of their homes for festivals and weddings. In the 1960s artists began painting on paper, and it became known around the world.
skills.practisedBy: Traditionally the women of Mithila families, who passed the style from mother to daughter.
techniqueSteps: Draw a double outline of your design.
Fill the space between the lines with small patterns like dots and dashes.
Colour the shapes with flat, bright colours.
Leave no empty space: fill gaps with flowers, leaves or lines.
skills.whyItMatters: It keeps the stories, festivals and nature of Mithila alive in pictures anyone can enjoy.

image.alt: Illustration of two fish surrounded by flowers in the Madhubani style

skills.name: Warli painting
skills.blurb: Simple white figures made of circles, triangles and lines that show village life, dancing and farming.
skills.history: Warli painting is made by the Warli community of Maharashtra. It was painted on the mud walls of homes, often for weddings and harvests, using white paste made from rice.
skills.practisedBy: The Warli Adivasi (tribal) community of the Sahyadri foothills.
techniqueSteps: Start with a dark brown or red background.
Draw people with two triangles joined at the tips, a circle head and line arms.
Add trees, animals and houses with simple shapes.
Show a circle of dancers (the tarpa dance) in the middle.
skills.whyItMatters: It records how a community lives with nature, using only a few shapes and one colour.

image.alt: Illustration of white Warli stick figures dancing in a circle on a brown background

skills.name: Jaipur blue pottery
skills.blurb: Shiny pots and tiles painted in cobalt blue and turquoise, with flowers and birds.
skills.history: Blue pottery is linked with Persian and Mughal glazed tile work and became well known in Jaipur. Unlike most pottery it is not made from clay but from a dough of quartz powder, glass and other materials.
skills.practisedBy: Families of craftspeople in and around Jaipur.
techniqueSteps: Mix quartz powder, glass powder and natural gum into a dough.
Shape it in a mould and let it dry.
Paint flowers and patterns in blue, using colours from cobalt and copper.
Glaze it and fire it in a kiln at a low temperature.
skills.whyItMatters: It is a rare type of pottery, and only a small number of workshops still make it by hand.

image.alt: Illustration of a round blue and white pot with flower patterns

skills.name: Terracotta pottery
skills.blurb: Red-brown clay shaped by hand or on a wheel, then baked to make pots, lamps and animal figures.
skills.history: People in India have made fired clay objects for thousands of years. Bankura in West Bengal is famous for its tall terracotta horses, and many villages still make clay pots and diyas for everyday use and festivals.
skills.practisedBy: Potter (kumhar) families in villages across India.
techniqueSteps: Clean the clay and knead it until smooth.
Shape it on a spinning wheel or by hand.
Let it dry slowly in the shade.
Bake it in a kiln until it turns hard and red-brown.
skills.whyItMatters: Clay is natural and local, so terracotta is one of the most earth-friendly crafts.

image.alt: Illustration of a red-brown terracotta horse and a clay pot

skills.name: Dhokra metal casting
regions: Parts of Odisha, West Bengal and Jharkhand
skills.blurb: Small metal figures of animals and people, made using wax and clay in a very old method.
skills.history: Dhokra uses the lost-wax method of casting metal, one of the oldest known ways of making metal objects. The famous 'Dancing Girl' from Mohenjo-daro was made using lost-wax casting.
skills.practisedBy: Metalsmith communities in central and eastern India.
techniqueSteps: Make a clay core in the rough shape.
Cover it with thin threads of wax to add detail.
Coat the wax in more clay and heat it so the wax melts away.
Pour melted brass into the empty space, cool it, and break the clay.
skills.whyItMatters: Every piece is one of a kind, because the mould is broken to get it out.

image.alt: Illustration of a golden metal elephant with spiral wire patterns

skills.name: Bagru block printing
skills.blurb: Patterns printed on cloth by hand using carved wooden blocks and natural dyes.
skills.history: Bagru is a village near Jaipur where the Chhipa community has printed cloth by hand for generations. It is known for earthy colours and the dabu method, where mud is used to block dye from parts of the cloth.
skills.practisedBy: The Chhipa community of printers in Bagru.
techniqueSteps: Wash the cloth and prepare it to take dye.
Dip a carved wooden block into colour.
Press it firmly onto the cloth, lining up each print with the last.
Dry the cloth in the sun and wash it to fix the colours.
skills.whyItMatters: It uses natural dyes and hand skill that machines cannot fully copy.

image.alt: Illustration of a wooden printing block next to a cloth with repeated flower prints

skills.name: Kalamkari
skills.blurb: Cloth painted or block-printed with plant dyes, showing trees, flowers and stories.
skills.history: Kalamkari means 'pen work'. In Srikalahasti, artists draw freehand with a bamboo pen to tell stories from epics. In Pedana, near Machilipatnam, the designs are printed with wooden blocks.
techniqueSteps: Soak cotton in a mix that helps it hold dye.
Draw or print the outline in black.
Fill in colours made from plants, such as indigo and madder.
Wash the cloth in flowing water and dry it in the sun.
skills.whyItMatters: It shows how plants can give long-lasting colour without harsh chemicals.

image.alt: Illustration of a Kalamkari tree of life with curling leaves and a peacock

skills.name: Kanjeevaram silk weaving
skills.blurb: Heavy silk sarees woven on handlooms, with wide borders and gold thread.
skills.history: Kanchipuram in Tamil Nadu has been a weaving town for centuries. Its silk sarees are famous for strong silk and borders woven separately and joined firmly to the body of the saree.
techniqueSteps: Dye the silk threads in bright colours.
Set up the long threads (warp) on the loom.
Pass the cross threads (weft) through by hand, line by line.
Weave in zari (metal thread) to make the border and patterns.
skills.whyItMatters: One saree can take many days of careful work, showing great patience and skill.

image.alt: Illustration of a folded silk saree with a gold temple-style border

skills.name: Ikat weaving
skills.blurb: Threads are tie-dyed before weaving, so the pattern appears as the cloth is made.
skills.history: In ikat, weavers tie and dye the threads in planned patterns before they go on the loom. Odisha's Sambalpuri ikat and Telangana's Pochampally ikat are two well-known styles.
skills.practisedBy: Weaving communities in Odisha and Telangana.
techniqueSteps: Plan the pattern on paper.
Tie small bundles of thread tightly so the dye cannot reach those parts.
Dye the threads, then untie them.
Weave carefully so the coloured parts line up into the pattern.
skills.whyItMatters: It needs maths, planning and patience, all at once.

image.alt: Illustration of ikat cloth with soft-edged zig-zag diamond patterns

skills.name: Sitar & tabla
skills.blurb: The sitar's ringing strings and the tabla's talking drums are at the heart of Hindustani music.
skills.history: The sitar and tabla are key instruments in Hindustani classical music of North India. Music is often taught through the guru–shishya tradition, where a student learns closely from a teacher over many years.
skills.practisedBy: Musicians across North India, often trained in family traditions called gharanas.
techniqueSteps: Learn to sit with good posture and hold the instrument.
Practise a basic rhythm cycle (taal), like teentaal with 16 beats.
Learn the notes Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni.
Play simple patterns again and again with a teacher.
skills.whyItMatters: It trains listening, memory and patience, and connects you to centuries of music.

image.alt: Illustration of a sitar with a long neck beside a pair of tabla drums

skills.name: Carnatic veena
skills.blurb: A large stringed instrument with a deep, warm sound, played in Carnatic music.
skills.history: The veena is one of the oldest instruments mentioned in Indian texts. The Saraswati veena is used in Carnatic classical music of South India, and the goddess Saraswati is often shown holding one.
skills.practisedBy: Musicians across South India, usually trained by a guru.
techniqueSteps: Learn to sit and rest the veena across your lap.
Press the strings on the frets with your left hand.
Pluck with your right hand to play the basic exercises (sarali varisai).
Learn simple songs, then ragas with your teacher.
skills.whyItMatters: It carries the sound of South Indian music and its songs from one generation to the next.

image.alt: Illustration of a veena with a round wooden body and curved neck

skills.name: Kathak
skills.blurb: A storytelling dance with fast spins, rhythmic footwork and ankle bells.
skills.history: The word Kathak comes from 'katha', meaning story. Storytellers in North India told tales through dance. Over time it grew in temples and royal courts into the dance we see today.
skills.practisedBy: Dancers trained in gharanas such as Lucknow, Jaipur and Banaras.
techniqueSteps: Learn the basic stance and hand positions.
Practise tatkaar, striking the feet in time with the beat.
Add chakkars (spins) slowly and safely.
Use your face and hands to tell a small story.
skills.whyItMatters: It joins music, rhythm and storytelling, and it keeps old stories alive.

image.alt: Illustration of a Kathak dancer spinning with a flared skirt

skills.name: Bharatanatyam
skills.blurb: A classical dance from Tamil Nadu with strong poses, clear footwork and expressive hands.
skills.history: Bharatanatyam developed in the temples of Tamil Nadu. In the 20th century, artists such as Rukmini Devi Arundale, who founded Kalakshetra in Chennai, helped bring it to stages around the world.
skills.practisedBy: Dancers trained by gurus across India and the world.
techniqueSteps: Learn the aramandi, a half-sitting position with knees bent outwards.
Practise adavus, the basic steps, with the beat.
Learn hand gestures called mudras.
Use expression (abhinaya) to show feelings and stories.
skills.whyItMatters: It builds strength and focus and keeps music, poetry and stories together.

image.alt: Illustration of a Bharatanatyam dancer in a half-sitting pose with arms outstretched

skills.name: Pongal (harvest dish)
skills.blurb: A dish of rice and lentils cooked during the Pongal harvest festival, sweet or savoury.
skills.history: Pongal is both the name of a harvest festival in Tamil Nadu and the dish cooked for it. Families boil new rice with milk until it bubbles over, which is a sign of plenty.
skills.practisedBy: Families across Tamil Nadu and Tamil communities around the world.
techniqueSteps: Wash rice and moong dal.
Cook them together with milk or water until soft.
For sweet pongal, add jaggery, ghee and cardamom.
With an adult, fry cashews in ghee and stir them in.
skills.whyItMatters: It connects food with farming, the seasons and saying thank you for the harvest.

image.alt: Illustration of a clay pot overflowing with rice, with sugarcane and a kolam pattern

skills.name: Makki di roti & sarson da saag
skills.blurb: Corn flatbread with slow-cooked mustard greens, a winter favourite in Punjab.
skills.history: In Punjab, mustard greens grow well in winter, and maize (makki) flour is used for flatbreads. The two are cooked together as a hearty seasonal meal, often shared with the whole family.
skills.practisedBy: Home cooks across Punjab, on both sides of the border.
techniqueSteps: Wash and chop mustard greens with a little spinach.
Cook them slowly, then mash them until smooth.
With an adult, make a tadka with ginger, garlic and onion.
Pat maize dough into rotis and cook them on a tawa.
skills.whyItMatters: It shows how food follows the seasons and the crops a region grows.

image.alt: Illustration of a round yellow corn roti beside a bowl of green saag
